## Findings by module

### module 4

- **refined** (ch-001.txt): Palmer's note on the chronicle's dating: the founder Bagoda's dates (AD 999) are the start of the list, but the chronicle itself gives lengths only, so any date before the late 1300s depends on the 1807 back-count, which the course should describe as the chronicle's own chronology not an independent date
- **refined** (ch-001.txt): Askia question: the translated Kano Chronicle names no Askia conquest of Kano or Katsina; Palmer's introduction says only that the Hausa states were tributary to Songhay and Bornu at different periods, with no date
- **contradicted** (ch-002.txt): Sulimanu (AD 1807-1819, a Fulani Sarki): the chronicle says Fulani chiefs refused to enter the Hausa palace, and Mallam Jibrin said Fulani would become like the Habe if they entered Hausa houses and had children; Palmer's chapter 1 reading says Habe means any conquered negro people, so the course should give both the Hausa-Fulani social line and Palmer's reading of the word
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Rimfa reigned AH 867-904 (AD 1463-1499), which fits Suyuti's letter and Magili's visit to Kano and Katsina; Bornu evidence puts Othman Kalnama's refuge in Kano at AD 1432 and the Chronicle says Abdulahi Burja (c. AD 1438) was the first Hausa Sarki to pay tribute to Bornu
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Under Abdulahi Burja (AD 1438-1452) Kano's Galadima Daudu raided the south and sent a thousand slaves a month to the Sarki, founded 21 towns each holding a thousand slaves, and Burja gave Bornu tribute, opened roads from Bornu, and first kept camels in Hausaland; this is the chronicle's clearest picture of Kano slave supply in the 1400s
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Rimfa (AD 1463-1499): the chronicle has a sharif, Abdu Rahaman, establish Islam in Kano after a soil test against Medina soil; it has the Sarki order a Friday mosque built where the sacred tree stood; Palmer dates Abdu Rahaman's visit near the Maghili visit already logged in chapter 1
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Palmer 1908 translation in JRAI vol 38 pp 58-98; the MS was found at Sabongari near Katsina, runs to the 48th king Mohammed Belo, and was probably written 1883-1893 on internal evidence, copying an older lost record
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Palmer dates the reigns by working back from the Fulani entry into Kano in 1807 (AH 1222); he calls the reign lengths weak evidence alone but says the Chronicle is roughly accurate except for the earliest kings
- **note** (ch-001.txt): The Chronicle places Yaji (AD 1349-1385) and the arrival of Wangarawa Mandingo from Melle bringing Islam; Palmer links this to Mansa Musa's 1326 pilgrimage and a 1373 Melle campaign at Tekidda, but calls the link probable, not proven, and says Magili was usually held the first Muslim missionary to reach Kano
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Palmer's three layers: Negro base, Hamitic invaders from north and east, and late indirect Semitic influence; Libyo-Berber tombs on the Niger and in the Kano and Katsina valleys suggest Ghana-linked influence between 500 BC and AD 400 (his estimate)
- **note** (ch-001.txt): About AD 1000 an alien eastern people ruled the Hausa states until the Fulani took over in 1807; Palmer says habe means any conquered negro people, so hausa should be used for the post-1000 population. Origin stories conflict: Baghdad and horse introduction in Daura, slaves of the Sultan of Bornu (via El Bakri), Tatars and Mongols
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Palmer links the Sa or Sau serpent clans, who moved west of the Niger in the 12th century (Susu, Sarrakole, Sosso names) and brought the horse, to the Daura snake legend; he presents this as a suggestion, and Bornu fought the Sau in 1346-1349
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Source caution: Palmer's translation is the only text, the Arabic is slipshod and stylised, authorship is unknown, and the Dalla and Barbushe material is pre-Islamic ritual legend recorded by a Muslim writer; Palmer thanks Temple, Alexander and Reid for checking
- **note** (ch-001.txt): The chronicle's reign list runs from Bagoda (AH 389-455, AD 999-1063) to Yaji, with each reign length given in years; the list has pagan chiefs ruling Kano before Bagoda, and Bagoda's line claims descent from Bayajidda through Bauwo
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Warisi and Gijimasu built walls with eight gates (c. AD 1095-1134), and Gijimasu's son Tsaraki (Yusa) completed the walls; the chronicle says the old pagan grove and its sacrifices were defended by seeking gifts and then force, and the gate-building is given as a sign of the new city
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Naguji (AD 1194-1247) is the chronicle's first Sarki to collect a land tax of one-eighth of the crop; Yusa's reign has shields first in use (Kano dating: AD 1136-1194)
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Tsamia (AD 1307-1343) is recorded as the time the Tchibiri cult was practised and horns first used in Kano; the chronicle's account of the sacred grove ends with its destruction by Bajeri and Tsamia's men, a point the course can use to show the state-religion conflict in the source
- **note** (ch-001.txt): In Yaji's reign (AD 1349-1385) Wangarawa Mandingo arrived from Melle with about forty scholars under Abdurahaman Zaite, and Yaji ordered prayer across Kano; a mosque was built beneath the sacred tree, and the Sarkin Gazarzawa opposed prayer, so the chronicle shows Islam arriving by royal order and resisted by local chiefs
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Yaji's campaign against Santolo (chunk 3) is told with a Muslim prayer vigil, a traitor (Kosa) naming the defenders, and the Madawaki title as reward; the chronicle says Yaji died at Kworarafa or Kano, and the song in his praise is quoted as a source for conquest by tribute
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Kanajeji (AD 1390-1410) is the first Hausa Sarki to adopt lifidi, iron helmets and mail after heavy losses at Umbatu; the chronicle has him restore the Tchibiri cult by cutting a branch, killing a red snake and making drums from its skin, with forty days in the water; the source thus records a deliberate return to older rites as a war tool
- **note** (ch-001.txt): Dagachi (in Dauda's reign, AD 1421-1438) came from South Bornu with horse drums, trumpets, flags and guns; the chronicle also says Queen Amina of Zaria, after conquering as far as Kworarafa and Nupe, first brought eunuchs and kola to Hausaland; the guns line is early for the usual gun dates and should be taken as a claim
- **note** (ch-001.txt): The chronicle records a Sarki (Dakauta) who was dumb and was deposed after one night, and a short reign (Atuma, seven days); under Yakubu (AD 1452-1463) the chronicle says Fulani came to Hausaland from Melle, which the course should not read as the nineteenth-century Fulani jihad
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Under Yakubu (AD 1452-1463) the chronicle has salt becoming common, Gwanja merchants coming to Katsina, and Arab settlers in Kano and Katsina; the trade pattern is in the source, though its date is the chronicle's own
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Kisoki (AD 1509-1565 by the chronicle's lengths; the printed A.D. 1065 is an OCR slip) is the reign with Shehu Tunus, Shehu Abdu Salam and the books brought to Kano, Shehu Karaski and Maguni from Bornu, and a Friday mosque built for the Kano scholars; the course can use this for a Kano scholarly network before 1600
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Abubakr Kado (AD 1565-1573) reigned while Katsina men reached the walls of Kano and the countryside was emptied; the chronicle says Mallam Sherif, Tamma, Gesui and Wuri came from Lagos, though some say Bagarmi, and Tamma settled at Godia; the origin of these mallams is unclear in the source itself
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Mohamma Zaki (AD 1582-1618): the chronicle reports a famine lasting eleven years, Kworarafa raids, and a Maghrebi scholar, Shehu Abubakr, who promised victory over Katsina for a price of wealth and gifts; the chronicle's victory at Guraji (about 400 horses taken) is the one battle with a specific number in this stretch
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Footnote 2 in ch-002 records the Koran wrapped in goat-skin (dirki), later cow hide up to forty skins, and Alwali stopping the practice in the Koran opening episode; a useful note on how the Chronicle records religious practice, but the footnote is the translator's, not the chronicler's
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Caution on the Kano chronology: the OCR gives A.D. 1065 and A.D. 1509-1065 for Kisoki; source_verify and the course must use 1565 and state that the printed date is an OCR error, not a source reading
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Kutumbi (chronicle dates AD 1623-1648; the printed 4648 is an OCR slip) is the first Sarki to collect jangali, a cattle tax, from Fulani clans (100 cows from the Jafunawa, 70 from the Baawa, and others): a fiscal source for Fulani pastoral wealth in the 1600s, in the chronicle's own words
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Kutumbi's court is described as having six hundred horses, ninety mailed horsemen, forty drums, and a hundred eunuchs; the chronicle's power list shows a favourite (Kalina Atuman) and a Wazir-like rule, which is a useful picture of court politics in Kano
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Sharefa (AD 1703-1731) is said to be the reign when cowries first came to Hausaland, and the chronicle lists seven practices of extortion (karo, rinsua, matafada, jizia on maidens at marriage and others); this is a source claim about money and tax, and the cowrie date is the chronicle's, not an independent one
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Kumbari (AD 1731-1743) had fierce wars with Gobir, shields brought from Nupe, and a jizia collection so heavy that Arab traders left Kano for Katsina and the poorer townspeople fled; a counsellor (Turaki Kuka Tunku) warned against it, and the Sarki listened
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Dadi (AD 1670-1703) faced a Kworarafa attack that killed about ninety-seven Sarkis men, and the Sarki fled to Daura; the chronicle says Tchibiri was carried to the battle and the Kworarafa failed to seize it, showing the cult in war again
- **note** (ch-002.txt): OCR caution: the printed dates here include A.D. 1623-4648 and A.H. 1059 with a Lagoni-type place name; do not cite dates from this chunk without checking the scan, and the Lagoni place name in the earlier ch-002 section is not clear enough to use
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Yaji (AD 1753-1768) is the first Sarki with a guard of musketeers in Kano, a practice the chronicle says lasted ever since; Babba Zaki (AD 1768-1776) raided Auyau and Burumburumi and forced his chiefs to war against their judgment; the chronicle dates musketeers to the late 1700s, which matches the course's gun-trade lessons only loosely
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Alwali (AD 1781-1807, the last Hausa Sarki) faced famine, a dispute over Dirki (a Koran hidden in goatskin, which he opened and found a Koran inside), and then the Fulani conquest in the name of reviving Islam; he fled to Zaria and then Rano and was killed at Burum-Burum; the chronicle's own account of the 1807 takeover is first-hand from a Hausa side
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Dabo (AD 1819-1846) is called the sacker of towns; he took Rano and Sankara, shaved his head only after a sack, and built a power base around Galadima Ango; the chronicle's own verses (sung praise of his horses) show the court's chronicle style, useful for the source-criticism lesson
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Abdulahi (AD 1855-1883) reigned during a great famine and a long war with Umbatu, and the chronicle says he cut off the hands of thieves and killed robbers; the printed dates end at 1883, the chronicle's own last date, matching Palmer's remark on the MS being written in the 1880s
- **note** (ch-002.txt): OCR caution: the chunk prints 'Dirki' and 'Dirli' and 'Alwali' with variant spellings, and the note '(Dirki is nothing but the Koran)' appears in the translator footnote; any course quote should give the translator's wording with the chapter, not a new spelling
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Abdulahi (AD 1855-1883) had guns fired whenever he mounted his horse until it became a custom; the chronicle's Abdulahi reign also shows palace slaves becoming near free men, and a Galadima Yusufu rising and falling; a useful picture of court slavery in the 1800s
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Mohammed Belo (AD 1883-1892) is the last reign in the chronicle; the printed reign ends the MS and fixes Palmer's date of writing to the 1880s, and Belo's chief minister Saikin Fada (Waziri) ran the state as Belo's friend
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Plate note: Palmer's Fig 3 is a tomb of an early Katsina king, which he says is similar to the tombs El Bekri described at Ghana (p. 61); the course can cite this as Palmer's own comparison, which he presents as suggestive, not proved
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Plate note: Fig 2 shows a sacred crocodile at Musawa, Katsina, with a ring through its nose, said to be 200 years old; the source records a living animal cult in the 1900s, useful to show how older religion survived into the colonial period
